note: Preregistered experiment, 40 percent time reduction and 18 percent quality gain on professional writing tasks.
title: Experimental evidence on the productivity effects of generative artificial intelligence

reading.body:
In a preregistered experiment on professional writing tasks, generative AI cut completion time by 40 percent while improving output quality by 18 percent.

Preregistration matters methodologically, it means the hypotheses and analysis plan were fixed before the results came in, which rules out one of the most common ways studies overstate an effect after the fact. Getting both a large time reduction and a quality improvement, rather than a speed and quality tradeoff, is also a stronger result than either finding alone.

The paper's tasks were professional writing specifically, so the 40 percent and 18 percent figures should not be assumed to generalize to other kinds of work without their own testing.

explain_beginner: This study asks whether letting a professional use ChatGPT for a real writing task makes that task faster and better, and whether the benefit is the same for everyone or mostly helps people who were struggling before. The researchers recruited college educated professionals, people who write for a living in roles like marketing, HR, consulting, and grant writing, and had each of them complete two writing tasks specific to their own occupation, randomly letting some use ChatGPT and not others. This matters because a lot of early claims about AI boosting productivity came from surveys or small demos rather than a controlled test with real professional tasks and independent grading. The study found that ChatGPT access cut the time spent on a task substantially and raised the graded quality of the output, and the people who benefited most were those who had been the weakest writers beforehand, essentially closing much of the gap between strong and weak performers. It does not tell us what happens when this scales across an entire labor market, including whether demand for these writing services changes, and the authors note that real world adoption outside the lab was still far from universal even among people who had just been shown how useful it was.
explain_business: The direct business relevance is a specific, experimentally measured range, roughly 40 percent faster task completion and 18 percent higher quality scores for professional writing tasks, which gives a concrete benchmark against which to judge an internal generative AI writing pilot rather than relying on anecdote. The equity relevant finding is that these tools appear to help weaker or newer writers the most, narrowing performance gaps across a team, which is relevant to how a manager might target training or access rather than assuming senior staff benefit equally. The important caveat for planning is the adoption gap the study itself surfaces, even after being shown the tool's benefit in a controlled setting, a large share of participants were not using it on the job weeks later, which points to a real friction between demonstrated capability in a study and actual daily use, often due to unfamiliarity or workplace access restrictions rather than the tool's capability. This applies now to any organization with knowledge workers doing occupation specific writing, and the harder question the study leaves open, how the whole labor market and pricing for these services shifts once adoption is widespread, is not one a single company's pilot can answer on its own.
explain_practitioner: The design was a randomized controlled experiment run on the Prolific platform with college educated professionals completing two occupation specific writing tasks each, mid task random assignment moved half the participants into a ChatGPT access condition while the rest served as controls, and outputs were graded independently. Time spent on the assigned task fell by about 40 percent for the treatment group, and average grades rose by about 18 percent, with the paper noting that most of the quality gain reflected the quality of ChatGPT's own draft output rather than participants meaningfully editing or improving on it. The most notable distributional result was that the gap between the weakest and strongest performers in the control group nearly disappeared in the treatment group, with the tool bringing most participants close to what the best unaided writers had achieved. As a limitation, the authors are explicit that their controlled task based estimates cannot capture general equilibrium effects, changes in the price or demand for these services once the whole market has access to the tool, and they report that only about 34 to 42 percent of participants said they had actually used ChatGPT at their real job weeks after the study, showing a real gap between demonstrated capability and workplace adoption.
